nodes.body: ## Pull request overview Updates the `copilot-check` skill documentation to turn it from a single-pass “fetch and report” helper into an automated verify→fix→re-review loop, plus a first-round front-load step to reduce iteration churn. **Changes:** - Defines a multi-round autonomy model (verify/refute first, class-level sibling scan, 80/20 auto-fix gate, convergence + unattended-round cap). - Adds “front-load” steps (semantic-ripple grep + optional first-round `/code-review` input gating). - Documents GraphQL-based re-request + background review watcher to drive automatic re-review rounds. --- 💡 Add Copilot custom instructions for smarter, more guided reviews. Learn how to get started.

## Pull request overview

Copilot reviewed 2 out of 2 changed files in this pull request and generated 5 comments.

`allowed-tools` includes `Skill`, but the design doc for this feature specifies widening to `Bash, Read, Glob, Grep, Edit, Write, Task` (no `Skill`). No other skill in this repo lists `Skill` in `allowed-tools`, so keeping it here risks the skill header drifting from the plan and/or using an unsupported tool name.

This references `copilot-instructions.md`, but earlier the rubric file is named `.github/copilot-instructions.md`. Using two different paths for the same rubric is confusing when following the runbook.

Hard-coding an opaque GraphQL node id as a “globally stable fallback” is brittle and risks requesting reviews from the wrong identity if GitHub changes IDs. Since the text already says the bot id is derivable from the prior review author, it’s safer to remove the fallback and explicitly stop/report if the Bot.id can’t be obtained.

The “high-water mark” command can return `null` when there has been no Copilot review yet, which then risks breaking the later watcher comparison if the harness substitutes `null` into `hwm`. Also, this step claims to record the head SHA but the snippet only captures review id/submitted_at.

This thread-resolution query resolves *all* unresolved Copilot-authored threads, regardless of whether the thread was actually replied to in this run. That contradicts the “Only resolve threads that were actually replied to” rule and can prematurely resolve open Copilot threads if the flow pauses or skips any comment. Consider filtering to threads whose *last* comment is not Copilot (i.e., has a human reply) before resolving.

The bot-id derivation query only looks at `reviews(last:10)`. On PRs with many reviews, Copilot may fall outside the last 10, forcing the flow onto the hard-coded fallback more often (or failing to derive at all if the fallback is removed later). Increasing the window reduces fragility without changing behaviour.

The comment-thread fetch prints `.line`, but GitHub review comments can have `line: null` (e.g., outdated diffs). That can make the later File:Line reporting ambiguous. Prefer falling back to `.original_line` (or `.position`) so the runbook consistently produces a usable location.

The thread-resolution jq filter only checks that the last comment is *not* Copilot, but the inline comment says it is “OUR reply”. That’s a documentation mismatch that could mislead future edits (a non-Copilot reply could also be from someone else).

Related to the jq filter above: this explanatory text claims the filter guarantees the most recent comment is “our” reply, but the actual predicate only guarantees “not Copilot”. Either tighten the predicate (e.g. compare to the actor login) or soften the wording to match what the snippet really enforces.

`reviewThreads(first:50)` will miss threads on PRs with >50 review threads, which could leave responded Copilot threads unresolved and cause noisy re-processing in later rounds. Bumping to the GraphQL max (`first:100`) reduces this fragility (full pagination would be ideal, but this is at least a safer default for the runbook snippet).

This says the Copilot bot node id is “always present here”, but the same block also documents a hard-coded fallback for bootstrap runs with no prior Copilot review. That’s internally inconsistent and could confuse readers about when the fallback is expected to be used.
